replication.target_description: Hypothesis to replicate and bet on: People are more willing to harm a stranger when he has been described in dehumanized terms rather than humanized terms when the motives are instrumental. To evaluate this hypothesis, the authors perform a t-test comparing the share of participants reporting that they would break the stranger’s thumb for money in dehumanized treatment versus the humanized treatment. The willingness to harm a stranger is higher in the dehumanized treatment compared to the humanized treatment (t = 2.26, p = 0.025); p. 8513.

n.sample_role: participants in focal analysis after exclusions
n.exclusions: Since the experiment was expected to take, on average, 5 minutes, we had a show-up fee of $1. As preregistered, we also collected data on the two other conditions (when motives to harm are moral) reported in the original paper for exploratory purposes (n = 888). In line with the original study’s result, the willingness to harm a stranger for immoral behavior in the dehumanized condition (m = 4.466, sd = 2.278; n = 431) does not statistically differ from the willingness to harm a stranger in the humanized condition (m = 4.455, sd = 2.316; n = 457); independent-samples t-test with equal variances: t(886) = 0.073, p = 0.942; n = 888. The interaction term of [humanized vs. dehumanized] x [instrumental vs. moral] turns out to be statistically insignificant in a two-way ANOVA (F(1, 1739) = 2.97, p = 0.061; η² = 0.002; n = 1743), similar as in the original study (where the interaction effect is described as “marginally significant”).
